OFFICIAL ACADEMIC REGULATIONS & EXAMINATION RULES
Academic Year: 2024-2025 | B.Tech Programs
1. Attendance Regulations:
Students must secure a minimum of 75% aggregate attendance across all registered courses in a semester to be
eligible to appear for the End-Semester Examination. A condonation of up to 10% (between 65% and 74%) may be
granted on medical grounds subject to approval by the Academic Council.
2. Evaluation & Examination Pattern:
Continuous Internal Assessment (CIA) accounts for 40% weightage (2 Mid-Term Tests of 20 marks each,
Assignments/Quizzes of 10 marks, normalized to 40). End-Semester Examination accounts for 60% weightage
(3-hour comprehensive theory paper). Minimum passing marks are 40% in End-Semester Exam and 40% aggregate.
3. 10-Point Grading System:
The institution follows a 10-point Letter Grading Scale: O (Outstanding, 90-100%, Grade Point 10), A+ (Excellent,
80-89%, Grade Point 9), A (Very Good, 70-79%, Grade Point 8), B+ (Good, 60-69%, Grade Point 7), B (Above
Average, 55-59%, Grade Point 6), C (Average, 50-54%, Grade Point 5), P (Pass, 40-49%, Grade Point 4), F (Fail,
below 40%, Grade Point 0).
4. Degree Credit Requirements:
The total number of credits required for the award of the B.Tech Degree in Computer Science & Engineering (CSE) is
160 credits distributed across 8 semesters.

DEPARTMENT OF COMPUTER SCIENCE & ENGINEERING
OFFICIAL CURRICULUM & SYLLABUS HANDBOOK (2024-2028)
Branch: Computer Science & Engineering (CSE) | Degree: Bachelor of Technology (B.Tech)
Program Overview & Degree Structure
The Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering is a 4-year full-time academic program.
Total Degree Credits: 160 credits across 8 semesters.
Semester 3: Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201, 4 Credits)
Semester 5: Database Management Systems (CS301, 4 Credits), Operating Systems (CS302, 4 Credits), Computer
Networks (CS303, 3 Credits)
Semester 6: Compiler Design (CS304, 4 Credits), Web Technologies (CS305, 3 Credits), Software Engineering
(CS306, 3 Credits)
Semester 7: Machine Learning (CS401, 4 Credits), Artificial Intelligence (CS402, 3 Credits)
Semester 8: Cloud Computing (CS403, 3 Credits), Capstone Project & Internship (10 Credits)

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Course Code: CS301  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 5  |  Credits: 4 (L: 3, T: 1, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201), Discrete Mathematics (MA202)

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Course Objectives
? To understand the fundamental concepts of relational database management systems.
? To design database schemas using Entity-Relationship modeling and normalization techniques.
? To formulate complex database queries using Structured Query Language (SQL) and relational algebra.
? To examine transaction processing, concurrency control protocols, and database recovery mechanisms.
? To introduce NoSQL architectures and modern storage paradigms.

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Apply relational algebra and relational calculus to formulate declarative database queries.
? CO2: Design conceptual schema using Entity-Relationship diagrams and map them to relational schemas.
? CO3: Construct optimized SQL queries including joins, subqueries, views, and aggregate functions.
? CO4: Evaluate relational schemas using 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF functional dependency decomposition to eliminate
anomalies.
? CO5: Analyze ACID transaction properties, serializability, lock-based concurrency control, and write-ahead logging recovery.

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Introduction & Database System Architecture
Data models, schemas, and instances; Three-schema architecture and data independence; Database languages and interfaces;
Database users and administrators; Entity-Relationship model: entities, attributes, entity sets, relationships, constraints, weak entity sets,
Extended ER features (specialization, generalization, categorization).

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Unit 2
Relational Data Model & Relational Algebra
Relational model concepts, relational integrity constraints; Relational algebra operations: Selection, Projection, Union, Set Difference,
Cartesian Product, Rename, Natural Join, Outer Joins, Division; Tuple Relational Calculus and Domain Relational Calculus; Overview of
QBE.

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Unit 3
SQL & Query Processing
Data Definition Language (DDL) commands: CREATE, ALTER, DROP; Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands: INSERT,
UPDATE, DELETE; Advanced SELECT queries: nested subqueries, correlated subqueries, set operations, aggregate functions, GROUP
BY, HAVING; Integrity constraints, assertions, triggers, views; Overview of query optimization and cost estimation.

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Unit 4
Database Design Theory & Normalization
Informal design guidelines for relation schemas; Functional dependencies: Armstrong's axioms, closure of functional dependencies,
minimal cover; Normal forms based on primary keys: First Normal Form (1NF), Second Normal Form (2NF), Third Normal Form (3NF);
Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF); Multi-valued dependencies and Fourth Normal Form (4NF); Lossless join decomposition and
dependency preservation.

Course: DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS (CS301)
Section: Unit 5
Transaction Processing, Concurrency & Recovery
Transaction concepts, states, ACID properties; Schedules and serializability: conflict and view serializability; Concurrency control
techniques: Two-Phase Locking (2PL), strict 2PL, deadlock prevention and detection, timestamp ordering; Database recovery techniques:
deferred update, immediate update, shadow paging, write-ahead logging (WAL), checkpoints.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Course Code: CS302  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 5  |  Credits: 4 (L: 3, T: 1, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Computer Organization and Architecture (CS202), Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201)

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Course Objectives
? To introduce the core services, structures, and system call interfaces of modern operating systems.
? To explain process management, threads, multi-programming, and CPU scheduling algorithms.
? To study process synchronization mechanisms, critical-section problem solutions, and deadlock handling.
? To analyze contiguous and non-contiguous memory management, paging, segmentation, and virtual memory.
? To examine file system implementation, directory structures, and secondary storage disk scheduling.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Explain operating system structure, system calls, interrupt handling, and kernel architecture.
? CO2: Analyze and compare preemptive and non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithms for responsiveness and throughput.
? CO3: Implement synchronization primitives (semaphores, mutexes, monitors) to solve classic synchronization problems.
? CO4: Design and evaluate deadlock prevention, avoidance (Banker's Algorithm), and detection strategies.
? CO5: Demonstrate virtual memory techniques including page replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Optimal) and evaluate disk
scheduling.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
OS Overview & Process Concept
Role and purpose of operating systems, kernel architectures (monolithic, microkernel, hybrid), system calls, OS services; Process
concept: process states, Process Control Block (PCB), context switching; Threads: user-level and kernel-level threads, multithreading
models; Process scheduling queues, schedulers.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Unit 2
CPU Scheduling & Process Synchronization
Scheduling criteria: CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, response time; Scheduling algorithms: First-Come
First-Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), Priority Scheduling, Round Robin (RR), Multilevel
Queue Scheduling; Inter-process communication (IPC); Critical Section problem, Peterson's algorithm, hardware synchronization,
semaphores, mutex locks, monitors; Classic problems: Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, Dining Philosophers.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Unit 3
Deadlocks
Deadlock characterization: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait; Resource allocation graph (RAG); Deadlock
prevention strategies; Deadlock avoidance: safe state, Banker's algorithm for single and multiple resource instances; Deadlock detection
and recovery.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Unit 4
Memory Management & Virtual Memory
Logical versus physical address space, swapping, contiguous allocation, fragmentation (internal and external), paging, translation
lookaside buffer (TLB), multi-level paging, inverted page tables, segmentation; Virtual memory: demand paging, page fault handling, page
replacement algorithms (FIFO, Optimal, LRU, LFU, MFU), allocation of frames, thrashing and working set model.

Course: OPERATING SYSTEMS (CS302)
Section: Unit 5
Storage Management & File Systems
File concepts, access methods (sequential, direct, indexed), directory structures, file mounting and protection; File system structure,
allocation methods (contiguous, linked, indexed), free-space management; Secondary storage structure: disk structure, disk scheduling
algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK), RAID levels.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Course Code: CS303  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 5  |  Credits: 3 (L: 3, T: 0, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Data Communication Principles (CS204), Operating Systems (CS302)

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Course Objectives
? To build a solid understanding of layered network architectures (OSI 7-layer and TCP/IP protocol suites).
? To study framing, error detection/correction, and medium access control mechanisms.
? To master routing algorithms, subnetting, IPv4/IPv6 addressing, and congestion control.
? To explore transport protocols (TCP and UDP), flow control, reliability, and socket programming.
? To analyze key application layer protocols including DNS, HTTP, SMTP, and network security basics.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Differentiate OSI reference model and TCP/IP protocol stack layers and their respective duties.
? CO2: Apply error detection (CRC, checksum) and framing algorithms at the Data Link Layer.
? CO3: Formulate IPv4/IPv6 CIDR subnet masks and evaluate distance-vector and link-state routing protocols.
? CO4: Contrast TCP and UDP connection semantics, congestion control (AIMD, slow start), and flow control.
? CO5: Analyze client-server application protocols including DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, DHCP, and SMTP.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Introduction & Physical / Data Link Layer
Network topologies, PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN; Protocol layers: OSI reference model vs TCP/IP protocol suite; Physical layer transmission
media; Data link layer design issues: framing, error control, CRC, Hamming codes, flow control: Stop-and-Wait, Go-Back-N, Selective
Repeat ARQ; HDLC.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Unit 2
Medium Access Control (MAC) Sublayer
Multiple access protocols: Pure and Slotted ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA; IEEE 802.3 Ethernet standard, Fast Ethernet, Gigabit
Ethernet; IEEE 802.11 Wireless LAN architecture; Bridges, switches, VLANs.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Unit 3
Network Layer & Routing
Network layer design issues, store-and-forward packet switching; Routing algorithms: shortest path routing, Distance Vector Routing
(Bellman-Ford), Link State Routing (Dijkstra), hierarchical routing, OSPF, BGP; Congestion control principles; IP addressing: IPv4 classes,
CIDR subnetting, NAT, ARP, RARP, ICMP, IPv6 header format and transition strategies.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Unit 4
Transport Layer
Transport service primitives, socket addressing, multiplexing and demultiplexing; User Datagram Protocol (UDP): segment header,
checksum; Transmission Control Protocol (TCP): connection establishment (three-way handshake), termination, TCP segment structure,
flow control via sliding window, TCP congestion control: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery.

Course: COMPUTER NETWORKS (CS303)
Section: Unit 5
Application Layer & Security Fundamentals
Domain Name System (DNS): hierarchical namespace, resource records, resolution; Electronic mail: SMTP, POP3, IMAP; HyperText
Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2), HTTPS, cookies; Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP); Network security introduction:
symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, firewalls.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Course Code: CS304  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 6  |  Credits: 4 (L: 3, T: 1, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Formal Languages and Automata Theory (CS205), Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201)

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Course Objectives
? To explore the phases of a language translator and the construction of lexical analyzers.
? To develop top-down and bottom-up parsing techniques for Context-Free Grammars.
? To apply syntax-directed translation for intermediate code generation.
? To study code optimization algorithms and target machine code generation.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Construct deterministic finite automata and lexical analyzers using regular expressions.
? CO2: Design LL(1), SLR(1), LR(1), and LALR(1) parsing tables for context-free grammars.
? CO3: Formulate syntax-directed definitions (SDD) and generate intermediate representations like three-address code.
? CO4: Apply machine-independent optimizations including loop invariant code motion and common subexpression elimination.
? CO5: Generate optimized target machine instructions and implement register allocation using graph coloring.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Introduction to Compilers & Lexical Analysis
Phases of a compiler, passes, compiler construction tools; Role of lexical analyzer, tokens, patterns, lexemes; Regular expressions,
Thompson's construction to NFA, subset construction to DFA, minimization of DFAs; Lex/Flex tool specification.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Unit 2
Syntax Analysis (Top-Down & Bottom-Up Parsing)
Context-free grammars, derivations, parse trees, ambiguity; Top-down parsing: recursive descent, predictive LL(1) parsing, FIRST and
FOLLOW computations; Bottom-up parsing: shift-reduce parsing, operator precedence, LR parsing algorithms (SLR, canonical LR, LALR);
Yacc/Bison parser generator.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Unit 3
Syntax-Directed Translation & Intermediate Code
Syntax-directed definitions (SDD), synthesized and inherited attributes, evaluation orders for SDDs; Intermediate representations: syntax
trees, postfix notation, three-address code (quadruples, triples, indirect triples); Translation of expressions, type checking, boolean
expressions, control flow statements.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Unit 4
Run-Time Storage & Code Optimization
Storage organization, activation records, stack allocation of space, heap management, parameter passing mechanisms; Principles of code
optimization: basic blocks, flow graphs, loop optimization, common subexpression elimination, dead code elimination, copy propagation,
constant folding.

Course: COMPILER DESIGN (CS304)
Section: Unit 5
Code Generation & Register Allocation
Issues in the design of code generators; Target machine description; Simple code generator algorithm; Register allocation and
assignment, register allocation by graph coloring; Peephole optimization.

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Course Code: CS401  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 7  |  Credits: 4 (L: 3, T: 1, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Probability and Linear Algebra (MA201), Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201), Python for Data Science
(CS102)

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Course Objectives
? To introduce fundamental concepts of supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.
? To study mathematical foundations of regression, classification, and clustering algorithms.
? To evaluate model generalization, bias-variance tradeoff, and cross-validation methodologies.
? To introduce neural networks, deep learning architectures, and modern ML pipelines.

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Formulate supervised learning models including Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVMs.
? CO2: Analyze decision trees, random forests, and ensemble boosting techniques (AdaBoost, XGBoost).
? CO3: Apply unsupervised clustering (K-Means, Hierarchical) and dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE).
? CO4: Evaluate classification performance using precision, recall, F1 score, ROC-AUC, and cross-validation.
? CO5: Construct multi-layer perceptrons with backpropagation and explain regularizers (L1/L2, dropout).

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Foundations & Supervised Regression
Overview of machine learning, types of learning; Linear regression: hypothesis representation, ordinary least squares, gradient descent
(batch, stochastic, mini-batch); Polynomial regression; Overfitting, underfitting, bias-variance tradeoff; Regularization: Ridge (L2) and
Lasso (L1) regression.

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Unit 2
Supervised Classification Models
Logistic regression: sigmoid activation, log-loss cost function, decision boundaries; Naive Bayes classifier, Bayes theorem, Gaussian and
Multinomial variants; Support Vector Machines (SVM): maximal margin hyperplane, soft margin, kernel trick (RBF, polynomial kernels);
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN).

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Unit 3
Tree-Based Models & Ensemble Learning
Decision tree learning: ID3, C4.5, CART; Splitting criteria: entropy, information gain, Gini impurity; Tree pruning; Ensemble methods:
Bagging (Random Forest), Boosting (AdaBoost, Gradient Boost, XGBoost); Stacking and voting classifiers.

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Unit 4
Unsupervised Learning & Dimensionality Reduction
Clustering: K-Means algorithm, Elbow method, Silhouette score; Hierarchical clustering (agglomerative, divisive, dendrograms);
Density-based clustering (DBSCAN); Dimensionality reduction: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), singular value decomposition (SVD),
t-SNE.

Course: MACHINE LEARNING (CS401)
Section: Unit 5
Neural Networks & Model Evaluation
Biological vs artificial neurons, Perceptron learning rule; Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), forward propagation, activation functions (ReLU,
Sigmoid, Tanh, Softmax); Backpropagation algorithm, chain rule, loss functions; Evaluation metrics: confusion matrix, precision, recall,
F1-score, ROC and PR curves, k-fold cross-validation.

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Course Code: CS201  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 3  |  Credits: 4 (L: 3, T: 1, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Programming in C (CS101)

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Course Objectives
? To introduce asymptotic notations and complexity analysis of algorithms.
? To implement linear data structures: arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues.
? To master non-linear data structures: trees, binary search trees, AVL trees, and graphs.
? To apply classic algorithm design paradigms: divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming.

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Compute asymptotic time and space complexity using Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta notations.
? CO2: Implement singly, doubly, and circular linked lists, stacks, and queues for real-world problems.
? CO3: Construct binary trees, BSTs, and self-balancing AVL trees with tree traversals.
? CO4: Execute graph traversal algorithms (BFS, DFS) and minimum spanning tree algorithms (Prim, Kruskal).
? CO5: Design dynamic programming and greedy solutions (knapsack, Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall).

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Complexity Analysis & Linear Data Structures
Asymptotic notations: O, Omega, Theta; Arrays and matrices; Linked Lists: singly linked lists, doubly linked lists, circular linked lists;
Operations: insertion, deletion, searching, traversal.

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Unit 2
Stacks & Queues
Stack abstract data type, array and linked list implementation; Applications of stacks: infix to postfix conversion, postfix evaluation,
balanced parenthesis; Queue ADT: circular queues, double-ended queues (deque), priority queues.

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Unit 3
Trees & Binary Search Trees
Tree terminologies, binary trees, representations, binary tree traversals (inorder, preorder, postorder, level order); Binary Search Trees
(BST): insertion, deletion, searching; Balanced search trees: AVL trees, rotations; B-trees and heaps (min-heap, max-heap).

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Unit 4
Graphs & Graph Algorithms
Graph representations: adjacency matrix, adjacency list; Graph traversals: Breadth First Search (BFS), Depth First Search (DFS);
Topological sort; Minimum Spanning Trees: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms; Shortest paths: Dijkstra's algorithm.

Course: DATA STRUCTURES AND ALGORITHMS (CS201)
Section: Unit 5
Algorithm Design Techniques & Sorting
Divide and Conquer: Merge Sort, Quick Sort; Greedy algorithms: Fractional Knapsack, Huffman coding; Dynamic Programming: 0/1
Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence; Sorting algorithms: Insertion, Selection, Bubble, Radix sort; Hashing: hash tables, collision
resolution techniques.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Course Code: CS305  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 6  |  Credits: 3 (L: 3, T: 0, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Object-Oriented Programming through Java (CS203)

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Course Objectives
? To teach modern web architectural standards, semantic markup, and responsive stylesheets.
? To explore client-side scripting with JavaScript and DOM manipulation.
? To build RESTful web services and server-side applications.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Construct standards-compliant, accessible responsive layouts using HTML5 and CSS3.
? CO2: Write modern ES6+ JavaScript code handling events, asynchronous fetch calls, and DOM modifications.
? CO3: Develop backend server APIs using Node.js and Express with JSON payload exchanges.
? CO4: Integrate relational and document databases with backend web application routes.
? CO5: Implement web security best practices including CORS, CSRF, XSS protection, and JWT authentication.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
HTML5, CSS3 & Responsive Design
HTML5 semantic elements, forms, input types, audio and video tags; CSS3 selectors, box model, Flexbox, CSS Grid layout, media
queries, mobile-first design principles.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Unit 2
Client-Side Scripting with JavaScript (ES6+)
JavaScript syntax, variables (let, const), data types, functions, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring; DOM manipulation, event
listeners; Promises, async/await, Fetch API for AJAX communication.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Unit 3
Server-Side Programming with Node.js & Express
Node.js runtime environment, npm, event loop, modules; Express framework: routing, middleware, request and response objects, error
handling, serving static files.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Unit 4
RESTful API Architecture & Data Persistence
REST architectural constraints, HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), status codes, JSON serialization; Database connectivity
with MongoDB and MySQL; CRUD operations via ORMs.

Course: WEB TECHNOLOGIES (CS305)
Section: Unit 5
Web Security & Deployment
Web security vulnerabilities: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), SQL injection; Authentication &
Authorization using JWT and OAuth2; Deployment on cloud platforms, HTTPS, SSL/TLS certificates.

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Course Code: CS306  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 6  |  Credits: 3 (L: 3, T: 0, P: 0)
Prerequisites: None

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Course Objectives
? To introduce software development lifecycles and Agile engineering practices.
? To master requirements elicitation, SRS authoring, and architectural design modeling.
? To apply software testing methodologies and quality assurance standards.

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Select appropriate software process models (Waterfall, Spiral, Agile Scrum) for software projects.
? CO2: Draft formal Software Requirements Specifications (SRS) based on IEEE 830 guidelines.
? CO3: Design modular software architectures using UML class, use-case, sequence, and activity diagrams.
? CO4: Formulate black-box and white-box test cases including boundary value analysis and path coverage.
? CO5: Apply software maintenance, risk management, and project scheduling techniques (Gantt charts, PERT).

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Software Process Models
Nature of software, software engineering layers; Software Process Models: Waterfall, Incremental, Evolutionary, Spiral; Agile
development: Agile manifesto, Scrum methodology, sprint planning, user stories, extreme programming (XP).

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Unit 2
Requirements Engineering & Analysis
Requirements engineering tasks: inception, elicitation, elaboration, negotiation, specification, validation; Functional and non-functional
requirements; Use-case modeling; IEEE 830 standard Software Requirements Specification (SRS) documentation.

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Unit 3
Software Design & UML Modeling
Design concepts: abstraction, modularity, architecture, information hiding, functional independence (cohesion and coupling);
Object-Oriented design using UML: Class diagrams, Object diagrams, Sequence diagrams, Collaboration diagrams, Activity diagrams,
State machine diagrams.

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Unit 4
Software Testing Strategies & Techniques
Strategic approach to testing: unit testing, integration testing, validation testing, system testing; Black-box testing: equivalence partitioning,
boundary value analysis, cause-effect graphing; White-box testing: basis path testing, cyclomatic complexity, control structure testing;
Regression testing.

Course: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING (CS306)
Section: Unit 5
Software Project Management & Quality
Project metrics, software estimation: COCOMO II model; Project scheduling: Gantt charts, PERT/CPM; Risk management: identification,
projection, mitigation; Software Quality Assurance (SQA): ISO 9001, CMMI levels, software maintenance.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Course Code: CS402  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 7  |  Credits: 3 (L: 3, T: 0, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Data Structures and Algorithms (CS201), Discrete Mathematics (MA202)

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Course Objectives
? To provide foundations of intelligent agents and heuristic search strategies.
? To model knowledge representation and automated reasoning using first-order predicate logic.
? To explore planning algorithms and uncertainty management using Bayesian networks.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Formulate state-space search problems for rational agents in complex environments.
? CO2: Implement informed heuristic search algorithms including A* search and Greedy Best-First Search.
? CO3: Represent domain knowledge using First-Order Logic (FOL) and apply resolution refutation.
? CO4: Model probabilistic reasoning in uncertain domains using Bayesian Belief Networks.
? CO5: Design adversarial game-playing agents using Minimax algorithm with Alpha-Beta pruning.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Unit 1: Introduction
Introduction to AI & State-Space Search
Definitions of AI, Turing test, intelligent agents, agent architectures, PEAS classification, environment types; Problem formulation as
state-space search; Uninformed search strategies: Breadth-First Search (BFS), Depth-First Search (DFS), Uniform-Cost Search (UCS),
Iterative Deepening Search (IDS).

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Unit 2
Heuristic Search & Adversarial Games
Informed search strategies: Greedy Best-First Search, A* search, admissibility and consistency of heuristics; Local search: Hill climbing,
Simulated Annealing, Genetic Algorithms; Adversarial search: Game playing, Minimax algorithm, Alpha-Beta pruning, evaluation functions.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Unit 3
Knowledge Representation & Logic
Knowledge-based agents, propositional logic, inference rules, horn clauses; First-Order Logic (FOL): syntax and semantics, quantifiers,
unifications, forward chaining, backward chaining, resolution refutation theorem proving.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Unit 4
Classical Planning & Constraint Satisfaction
Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP): constraint propagation, backtracking search for CSPs, forward checking; Classical planning:
PDDL language, STRIPS operators, state-space planning, planning graphs.

Course: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (CS402)
Section: Unit 5
Reasoning under Uncertainty
Acting under uncertainty, probability axioms, joint probability distribution, conditional probability, Bayes' rule; Bayesian Belief Networks:
semantics, conditional independence; Exact and approximate inference in Bayesian networks.

Course: CLOUD COMPUTING (CS403)
Course Code: CS403  |  Branch: CSE  |  Semester: 8  |  Credits: 3 (L: 3, T: 0, P: 0)
Prerequisites: Operating Systems (CS302), Computer Networks (CS303)

Course: CLOUD COMPUTING (CS403)
Section: Course Objectives
? To study cloud delivery models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment architectures.
? To examine hypervisor virtualization and container technologies (Docker, Kubernetes).
? To analyze cloud storage, distributed file systems, serverless computing, and cloud security.

Course: CLOUD COMPUTING (CS403)
Section: Course Outcomes
? CO1: Differentiate cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment types (Public, Private, Hybrid).
? CO2: Analyze CPU, memory, and network virtualization techniques and hypervisors (Type 1 and Type 2).
? CO3: Deploy containerized microservices using Docker and manage container clusters with Kubernetes.

DATA STRUCTURES & ALGORITHMS HIGH-YIELD CHEAT SHEET
Algorithm Complexity Reference:
- Array Access: O(1) | Search: O(N) | Insertion/Deletion: O(N)
- Singly Linked List: Search O(N) | Insert/Delete at Head: O(1)
- Binary Search Tree (BST): Average Search/Insert/Delete O(log N) | Worst Case O(N) (skewed)
- AVL Tree / Red-Black Tree: Guaranteed Search/Insert/Delete O(log N) in worst case
- Hash Table: Average Search/Insert/Delete O(1) | Worst Case O(N) under high collisions
Sorting Complexities:
- Quick Sort: Best/Average O(N log N) | Worst Case O(N^2) | Space O(log N) | Not Stable
- Merge Sort: Best/Average/Worst O(N log N) | Space O(N) | Stable
- Heap Sort: Best/Average/Worst O(N log N) | Space O(1) | Not Stable
Graph Traversal:
- BFS: Uses Queue | Time O(V + E) | Finds unweighted shortest path
- DFS: Uses Stack / Recursion | Time O(V + E) | Finds connected components, cycles, topological sort
- Dijkstra: Greedy single-source shortest path | Time O((V + E) log V) with min-heap | Fails with negative edge weights!

DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS HIGH-YIELD CHEAT SHEET
Database Normalization Quick Rules:
1. 1NF (First Normal Form): All attributes must hold single, atomic values. No repeating groups or multi-valued columns.
2. 2NF (Second Normal Form): Table is in 1NF AND no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key (requires composite key to violate).
3. 3NF (Third Normal Form): Table is in 2NF AND no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on candidate keys (For every X -> Y, either X is a superkey or Y is prime).
4. BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form): Strictest form of 3NF. For every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X MUST be a Superkey!
Transaction ACID Rules:
- Atomicity: All-or-nothing execution guaranteed via Undo logging.
- Consistency: Preserves database integrity constraints before and after commit.
- Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere; guaranteed via 2-Phase Locking (2PL).
- Durability: Committed updates survive system crashes; guaranteed via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and Redo logging.

OPERATING SYSTEMS HIGH-YIELD CHEAT SHEET
Key Performance Metrics:
- Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time
- Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time
- Response Time = Time of first CPU allocation - Arrival Time
Deadlock: 4 Coffman Conditions (Must all hold simultaneously for deadlock):
1. Mutual Exclusion: Resources cannot be shared.
2. Hold and Wait: Process holds >= 1 resource while requesting others.
3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly seized.
4. Circular Wait: P0 waits for P1, P1 waits for P2, ..., Pn waits for P0.
Deadlock Avoidance - Banker's Algorithm Formulas:
- Need Matrix = Max Matrix - Allocation Matrix
- System is in a SAFE state if there exists at least one execution sequence where Need <= Available for every process.

OFFICIAL ACADEMIC REGULATIONS: REVALUATION PROCEDURE (Clause 8.1)
1. Answer Script Inspection:

2. Revaluation Application:
   - If dissatisfied after script inspection, a formal revaluation petition may be submitted within 10 days of photocopy receipt on payment of Rs. 1,000 per subject.
   - The script is re-examined independently by an external senior examiner.
   - If the variance in marks is 15% or higher, the average of the two closest marks is awarded. If marks increase by 10% or more, 50% of the revaluation fee is refunded to the student.

OFFICIAL ACADEMIC REGULATIONS: SUPPLEMENTARY EXAMS (Clause 8.2)
1. Supplementary / Arrear examinations are held twice annually:
   - Summer Supplementary Cycle: Conducted in July for odd and even semester courses.
   - Winter Supplementary Cycle: Conducted in January alongside regular odd semester examinations.
2. Eligibility:
   - Students who obtained an 'F' grade or 'Ab' (Absent on approved medical grounds) in regular exams are eligible to register.
   - Maximum 4 backlog subjects may be registered per supplementary session.
   - The original Continuous Internal Assessment (CIA) marks are carried forward.
   - The highest grade attainable in a supplementary exam is 'A' (Grade Point 8.0).

OFFICIAL ACADEMIC REGULATIONS: MALPRACTICE CLAUSES (Clause 9.1)
Categories of Examination Malpractice and Standard University Penalties:
- Category 1: Possession of unauthorized written notes, chits, formulas scribbled on hall tickets, calculators, or body parts.
  Penalty: Cancellation of performance in that specific subject, award of 'F' grade, and forfeiture of exam fee.
- Category 2: Possession or use of electronic gadgets (smartphones, smartwatches, Bluetooth earbuds, programmable calculators) inside examination hall.
  Penalty: Immediate confiscation of device, cancellation of performance in all registered subjects of the current semester, and mandatory disciplinary reprimand.
- Category 3: Impersonation / Proxy examination.
  Penalty: Expulsion of both the candidate and impersonator from the university, forfeiture of degree credentials, and registration of formal Police FIR.

COMPUTER NETWORKS HIGH-YIELD REVISION CHEAT SHEET
Subnetting Formulas:
- Number of Subnets created = 2^(subnet bits borrowed)
- Total IP Addresses per Subnet = 2^(host bits)
- Usable Host Addresses = 2^(host bits) - 2 (subtract 1 for Network ID, 1 for Directed Broadcast Address).
- Example: /26 mask (255.255.255.192) has 6 host bits -> 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable hosts per subnet.
OSI Layers & Protocols Quick Reference:
- Layer 7 Application: HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, FTP, SMTP, SSH
- Layer 4 Transport: TCP (reliable, connection-oriented, flow & congestion control), UDP (unreliable, connectionless, low latency)
- Layer 3 Network: IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF, BGP
- Layer 2 Data Link: Ethernet (802.3), Wi-Fi (802.11), ARP, switches, MAC addressing
- Layer 1 Physical: Bits, cables, hubs, repeaters.

COMPILER DESIGN HIGH-YIELD REVISION CHEAT SHEET
FIRST and FOLLOW Rules:
- FIRST(X):
  1. If X is terminal, FIRST(X) = {X}.
  2. If X -> epsilon, epsilon in FIRST(X).
  3. If X -> Y1 Y2 ... Yk, add FIRST(Y1) - {epsilon}. If Y1 can derive epsilon, add FIRST(Y2) - {epsilon}, and so on.
- FOLLOW(A):
  1. If A is start symbol, add '$' to FOLLOW(A).
  2. If B -> alpha A beta, add FIRST(beta) - {epsilon} to FOLLOW(A).
  3. If B -> alpha A or B -> alpha A beta where beta -> epsilon, add FOLLOW(B) to FOLLOW(A).
Parser Class Hierarchy:
- LL(1) < SLR(1) < LALR(1) < CLR(1)
- SLR(1): Uses LR(0) items + FOLLOW sets to resolve reduce actions.
- CLR(1): Uses LR(1) items [A -> alpha . beta, a] with lookaheads. Maximum parsing power among deterministic bottom-up parsers, but largest state count.
- LALR(1): Merges CLR(1) states with identical LR(0) cores. Reduces state size to equal SLR(1) without conflict explosion.
